analysis.one_liner: Gives refundable tax credits for buying health and long-term care insurance and restricts malpractice lawsuits.
analysis.headline: Sen. Mitch McConnell's health insurance tax credit bill died in the Senate Finance Committee in 1991 with zero cosponsors and never came to a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give refundable tax credits — covering up to 70% of premiums, capped at $2,500 a year — to people who buy their own health insurance because neither they nor a spouse has coverage through an employer. Low-income families could get the money up front as certificates to buy insurance. It also adds tax breaks for long-term care insurance, expands some Medicare benefits (in-home respite care, home IV drug therapy, broader home health care), funds rural health programs, and imposes new federal rules on medical malpractice lawsuits, including making the losing side pay attorney fees and ending joint liability. The bill was introduced by Sen. McConnell in February 1991, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured people who buy their own coverage — the credit is richest (70% of premiums, up to $2,500) for families earning under $25,000, with advance payments available to families below 1.49 times the poverty line. Seniors gain new Medicare benefits: up to 80 hours a year of in-home respite care for chronically dependent beneficiaries, coverage of home intravenous drug therapy, and broader home health services. Rural communities gain hospital payment changes, more National Health Service Corps scholarships and loan repayments, grants to county health departments for immunizations and maternal health, and higher funding for area health education centers. Long-term care insurance buyers and the industry gain from credits and favorable tax treatment. Doctors and malpractice insurers gain from liability limits.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured buyers, seniors, rural areas, insurers

how_it_helps.text: Creates a refundable tax credit for people without employer coverage: 70% of qualified health insurance premiums up to $2,500 for those with adjusted gross income under $25,000, phasing to zero at $40,000 [S3].
Lets families below 1.49 times the poverty line receive the credit in advance as certificates usable to buy health insurance through agreements between the Treasury and each state [S3].

Adds Medicare benefits: up to 80 hours a year of in-home respite care for chronically dependent beneficiaries and coverage of home intravenous drug therapy with no deductible, plus broader home health services [S3].

Requires reports on ending separate Medicare payment rates for rural versus urban hospitals — with a floor guaranteeing rural hospitals could not be paid less than their October 1991 levels — and funds rural prenatal care studies, county preventive health grants, and area health education centers [S3].

Creates a voluntary federal certification, with an emblem, for health insurance policies sold to seniors that meet minimum standards such as guaranteed renewability, limited preexisting-condition exclusions, and plain language [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers fund the credits, the Medicare expansions, and the rural health programs. People injured by medical malpractice bear the cost of the tort provisions: the losing side must pay the prevailing side's attorney fees (unless poor enough to qualify for Legal Services), and defendants are liable only for their own share of fault, which can leave an injured patient short when another wrongdoer cannot pay. Insurance companies' administrative role grows, since all subsidy money flows through private insurance purchases.

drawbacks.text: The tax-credit approach subsidizes private insurance premiums rather than guaranteeing coverage: a 70% credit capped at $2,500 leaves low-income families to pay the rest, and people who cannot afford any premium up front get nothing unless they navigate the certificate system [S3].

The malpractice title applies in every state and federal court, makes the losing party pay the winner's attorney fees, bars joint and several liability so each defendant pays only its own share of fault, and pushes parties toward arbitration or mediation that waives the right to go to court — all of which reduce what injured patients can recover [S3].

The tax code changes steer public money through private insurance companies: the health credit and the long-term care credit can only be used to buy commercial policies, and the long-term care title gives the industry new tax advantages including credits, employer-plan treatment, and penalty-free retirement withdrawals to pay premiums [S3].

Eliminating the separate rural and urban hospital payment rates could shift Medicare money between hospitals; the bill requires reports on how to do it but lets interim regulations take effect automatically if Congress does not act by December 1991 [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's help for uninsured people and seniors is real but modest and indirect — a capped tax credit that subsidizes premiums is cheaper for taxpayers than expanding public programs, but also leaves gaps in coverage. The strongest objection is the malpractice title: limiting defendants to their own share of fault and shifting attorney fees to losing patients makes it structurally harder for people harmed by medical negligence to be made whole, in exchange for costs savings that the bill itself claims mainly accrue through lower malpractice insurance and less defensive medicine. The rural health and Medicare provisions are largely beneficial and uncontroversial.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Finance Committee in February 1991, and it sat there — no hearings, no markup, no floor vote — until that Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Mitch McConnell introduced the Comprehensive American Health Care Act on February 21, 1991 [S5].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day, and no further action was ever taken on it [S5].
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, no one received the tax credits or new Medicare benefits — but malpractice plaintiffs also kept the existing liability rules, and the private insurance industry did not gain its new federally subsidized customer base. With zero cosponsors, the bill's death mostly reflects that neither party's leadership prioritized it; the health care debate of that Congress moved to larger proposals.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: insurers unexpanded, malpractice rules unchanged

for.name: Mitch McConnell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Finance Committee; it was his only action available — no cosponsors ever joined [S1][S5].

against.name: Daniel Patrick Moynihan
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee the bill was referred to, never scheduled action on it, so it died without a markup or vote.

against.name: The Senate
against.what_they_did: Never considered the bill after referring it to committee; no senator stepped forward to cosponsor it [S4][S5].

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record — a single Republican sponsor, and a Democratic-controlled committee that never acted.

industries.note: The bill creates refundable tax credits and advance certificates that can only be spent on private health insurance policies, making commercial insurers the permanent channel for the subsidy. Insurers gain new subsidized customers, and the uninsured gain help paying premiums.

The bill treats long-term care policies as health insurance for tax purposes, adds a refundable premium credit, lets employers pay premiums tax-free, and waives early-withdrawal penalties on retirement money used for premiums. Seniors considering coverage benefit from the subsidies alongside the industry.

The malpractice title limits each defendant to its own share of fault, shifts attorney fees to losing plaintiffs, and steers cases into arbitration. These changes reduce malpractice exposure and insurance costs, but run against injured patients' ability to collect full compensation.
Loser-pays fee shifting and the push toward binding alternative dispute resolution reduce malpractice contingency work and clients' day-in-court rights.

The bill directs a phase-out of separate rural-versus-urban Medicare payment rates with a floor guaranteeing hospitals could not be paid less than their October 1991 levels, and eases regulatory review for rural hospitals.
